title: A Second Chance at Risk: Supreme Court Ruling Threatens to Reimprison a Reformed Man
summary: Anthony Bailey, 61, has become a familiar face behind the wheel of an Indianapolis city bus. He spends weekends at barbecues and card tables, surrounded by grandchildren. It's a stark contrast to the 27 years he spent in a federal penitentiary for a 1997 bank robbery and carjackings. Released in 2024 under the compassionate release program—designed for inmates with extraordinary circumstances like severe illness or advanced age—Bailey had been granted a second chance. 'I'm a productive citizen, I work hard,' he says. But a late-May Supreme Court ruling has thrown his freedom into jeopardy. The justices limited compassionate release, stating that inmates serving sentences far longer than today's punishments are not automatically eligible. Bailey's case is one of about a dozen directly affected. His original sentence was inflated by stacked mandatory penalties—even though no shots were fired—a practice now softened by Congress, but not retroactively. Retired federal Judge John Gleeson, who has helped over 100 similarly situated inmates, calls such sentences 'indefensibly long.' Bailey's pro bono lawyer, Maryam Kanna, argues he poses no danger: 'He has a stable, happy life and is a really productive member of society.' Yet prosecutors are signaling they may move to reimprison him until 2050, when he would be nearly 86. For Bailey, the clock is ticking on a life he painstakingly rebuilt.
why_it_matters: This case shows how a single Supreme Court ruling can upend a person's future and raises questions about whether the justice system should prioritize fixed rules or the possibility of true rehabilitation—questions your generation may one day have to answer.

background_read: The U.S. prison system includes federal penitentiaries for serious federal crimes like bank robbery and carjacking. In the 1990s, tough-on-crime laws required judges to stack mandatory minimum sentences, so a person could receive decades even for a first offense without injuring anyone.

The First Step Act, signed into law in 2018, reduced some of those mandatory minimums, especially for certain firearm offenses, but did not apply to people already sentenced. That means thousands of inmates like Bailey remain in prison under the old, harsher rules.

Compassionate release is a separate tool that allows a judge to reduce a sentence for 'extraordinary and compelling reasons,' such as advanced age, terminal illness, or severe family circumstances. The Supreme Court (the highest federal court in the United States) recently limited who can qualify, stating that a long sentence originally legal at the time of sentencing is not, by itself, a reason for release.

The article also mentions retired federal Judge John Gleeson, who has fought for such inmates, and Bailey's pro bono lawyer—meaning she works for free—Maryam Kanna. They argue that a person who has rebuilt a stable life poses no danger to society.

perspectives.description: Bailey's story supports the idea that people can change. He works hard, pays taxes, and is a present grandfather. His supporters argue that keeping him in prison serves no public safety purpose and wastes resources, especially when his original sentence was inflated by laws now seen as too harsh.

perspectives.perspective: Negative / Prosecutorial and victims' rights viewpoint
perspectives.description: Prosecutors and some victims' advocates say that bank robbery and carjacking are serious, violent crimes. Even if no shots were fired, the terror inflicted on victims warrants lengthy punishment. They argue that reducing sentences retroactively undermines the finality of courts and may disrespect victims' pain.

The core tension is between 'rule of law' consistency and individualized justice. The Supreme Court's narrow reading of compassionate release upholds the principle that laws applied correctly at sentencing must stand, but it ignores how society's views on excessive punishment have evolved. Scholars debate whether this ruling will pressure Congress to make more sentencing reforms retroactive.

If Bailey is reimprisoned, it could deter others from seeking compassionate release and widen the gap between those who receive second chances and those who don't. On the other hand, widespread coverage of his case might mobilize advocates to push for new legislation that explicitly allows retroactive relief for long-ago sentences.
